blind_claims: A checkout request enters through a single public API gateway and fans out into two independent internal paths — Payments (synchronous, to Stripe and a Redis customer cache) and Orders (writing to Postgres and emitting an order-placed event that Notifications consumes asynchronously) — so the only synchronous work on the user's critical path is payment and order persistence, with everything downstream of the event decoupled.

A checkout request enters through one public gateway and fans out into two independent branches — Payments, which charges Stripe and reads a Redis customer cache, and Orders, which writes Postgres and emits an `order-placed` event that Notifications consumes asynchronously — so the only coupling between the synchronous purchase path and downstream notification work is the Kafka topic.

A checkout request enters through one public gateway and fans out into two independent branches — a synchronous payments path that hits Stripe and the Redis customer cache, and an orders path that writes to Postgres and emits an `order-placed` event to Kafka, with notifications happening asynchronously downstream rather than in the request itself.

tier_b:
One abstraction level per diagram: holds — client, two internal services, three data/event stores, one external SaaS and one worker are all one container-level tier, and every box is directly connected to the checkout request path the title names.

Architecture elements carry a type or technology line: every box has a second line, but the services get roles rather than technology ("Orders Service — internal service", "Payments Service — internal service", "Notifications — Kafka consumer"); only the stores name their tech (Postgres — orders database, Kafka — order-placed topic, Redis — customer cache). The three service boxes are where the rubric's "Orders — Postgres 16" upgrade is missing.

Sequence flows left to right, hierarchy top to bottom, entry point leading: this is a request sequence drawn top-to-bottom, and the entry point leads at the top right rather than leading the reading direction — the whole graph hangs off the right edge and the upper-left third of the canvas is empty, so the eye starts in blank space.

Relationship semantics stated once per diagram: not settled. The title says "Request Flow" (data flow), but the edge labels mix protocol (HTTPS, REST), action (writes, charge, reads customer, consumes) and event name (order-placed), and a second unstated channel rides along — dashed means async on Postgres→Redis, yet the equally async Kafka→Notifications "consumes" edge is solid.

A label sits beside the drawing it names: mostly fine — box labels sit inside shapes that have room. The pinch is under Orders and Payments, where "writes"/"order-placed" and "charge"/"reads customer" sit as tight adjacent pairs at the same y, and "cache warm (async)" is knocked out of the middle of its own dashed elbow, which is what makes that edge easy to miss (cf. the reader's "independent paths").

Band-comparison content weight, the small-multiples inversion, and "charts state the delta" do not apply — single panel, no small multiples, no chart.

Label beside the drawing, not on it: "cache warm (async)" is dropped directly onto its own dashed line, with dash fragments colliding with the text on both sides and the elbow corner reading as a stray glyph — move it above the segment.

Label beside the drawing (second instance): the two "REST" labels sit side by side at the same y, the left one far from the diagonal it belongs to, so the reader must trace strokes to tell which hop is which; "charge" likewise sits on top of the Payments→Stripe diagonal.

Relationship semantics stated once: the arrows mix two conventions — "reads customer" points toward Redis (dependency direction) while "consumes" points away from Kafka (data direction) — and neither title nor legend declares which is in force.

Sequence/hierarchy orientation: hierarchy runs top-to-bottom with Web App leading, which is right, but the entry column is pinned to the right margin, leaving the top-left third of the canvas empty so the entrypoint reads as tucked into a corner.

One abstraction level: clean — client, gateway, two services, three stores, one external API, one worker; every element is directly connected to the checkout scope the title states.

Type/technology line: every box carries a second line, but "internal service" under both Orders and Payments merely repeats its legend row instead of naming a runtime, and Postgres, Redis and Kafka carry no versions — "Postgres — orders database" names less than "Postgres 16".

Band content weight and the small-multiples inversion do not apply: single panel, no band. Charts state the delta does not apply: no chart.

**Panels of one band read at comparable content weight** — does not apply: the file is a single unframed panel, so there is no row to compare across, and per the rubric per-frame centring cannot fail.

**A label sits beside the drawing it names, not on top of it** — Mostly handled correctly: node names and their type lines sit inside boxes that have room for them, and mid-line arrow labels ("consumes", "cache warm (async)") are given a masked gap in the stroke rather than being overprinted. The one blemish is that the mask on the cache-warm line leaves a stranded dash fragment to the right of the label, which reads at a glance as a stray tick mark rather than part of the connector; a label placed just above the horizontal run would avoid cutting the line at all.

**One abstraction level per diagram** — Clean. Every element is a runtime participant of the checkout path: client, gateway, two services, three data/event stores, one external API, one worker. Nothing supporting has wandered in from deployment or code level, and the only outside-the-boundary element, Web App, is directly connected to the scope the title states.

**Sequence flows left to right, hierarchy top to bottom, entry point leading** — Orientation is top-to-bottom with Web App leading, defensible for a portrait doc-inline surface. What is off is horizontal placement: the entry column (Web App → API Gateway → Orders) is pinned to the right edge at x≈467 of a 648-unit canvas, so the reader's eye must start in the top-right corner and the flow then fans leftward and downward. The entire upper-left quadrant below the title is empty, and the title itself starts at x≈108 over that void, so the entry point leads but does not sit where the reader looks first.

**Relationship semantics are stated once per diagram** — This is the weakest Tier B item here. The title says "Request Flow", but the arrows carry three different semantics with nothing distinguishing them: synchronous calls ("HTTPS", "REST", "charge", "reads customer"), data writes ("writes", "cache warm"), and event flow ("order-placed", "consumes"). The legend types only the boxes and says nothing about what an arrow means, so a new backend engineer has to infer from each label whether an edge is a call, a write, or a subscription — and the solid stroke shared by the synchronous REST hops and the asynchronous Kafka "order-placed"/"consumes" hops actively works against that inference, while the one dashed edge implies dashed-means-async without the other async edges honouring it.

**Charts state the delta** — Does not apply; there is no chart, axis or ordered scale in the picture.

**The small-multiples inversion** — Does not apply; there are no consecutive panels, so there is no repeated layout to invert.

**Architecture elements carry a type or technology line** — Largely satisfied and the diagram's clear strength: all nine boxes carry a second line ("browser / client", "orders database", "order-placed topic", "customer cache", "Kafka consumer", "external API"). It stops short on the three boxes where it would matter most to a new engineer — "Orders Service / internal service", "Payments Service / internal service" and "API Gateway / public entrypoint" name the role rather than the technology, so the reader learns Postgres, Redis, Kafka and Stripe by name but not what the gateway or the two services are actually built on.
